category: PyAEDT: Desktop Session, Projects, Designs, Variables & Materials
description: The ansys.aedt.core application layer that sits above the modeler and solver: launching or attaching to an Electronics Desktop session (COM or gRPC, local or remote, graphical or headless), the session-wide settings and logger, project and design management, the variable manager with project ($) and design variables, datasets and output variables, the materials database and the native oDesktop/oProject/oDesign handles that stay reachable for anything PyAEDT does not wrap.

tools.name: Desktop (ansys.aedt.core.desktop.Desktop)
tools.description: The class that owns the Electronics Desktop process. Instantiating it launches a new AEDT session or attaches to a running one, and every application class (Hfss, Maxwell3d, Circuit, ...) created afterwards in the same script shares it. Use it explicitly when a script has to manage several designs or projects from one session, control autosave, submit cluster jobs or release the desktop once at the end; the application classes create an implicit Desktop when none exists.
tools.usage:
d = Desktop(version=None, non_graphical=False, new_desktop=True, close_on_exit=None,
            student_version=False, machine="", port=0, aedt_process_id=None)

parameters.name: version
parameters.description: AEDT release to start, as "2025.1", 2025.1 or 251. None uses the active setup or the latest installed version.

parameters.name: non_graphical
parameters.description: True launches AEDT without a window (the -ng mode). Required on headless Linux nodes and for batch scripts.

parameters.name: new_desktop
parameters.description: True always starts a fresh process; False attaches to a running session when one is found.

parameters.name: close_on_exit
parameters.description: Whether the desktop is closed when the Python object is released or the script ends.

parameters.name: student_version
parameters.description: True opens Ansys Electronics Desktop Student.

parameters.name: machine / port
parameters.description: gRPC target of an already running AEDT server (AEDT 2022 R2+). Leave empty for a local session.

parameters.name: aedt_process_id
parameters.description: Attach to a specific running AEDT process by PID.

parameters.name: Desktop methods
parameters.description: active_project(), active_design(), load_project(), save_project(), analyze_all(), enable_autosave()/disable_autosave(), clear_messages(), submit_job(), select_scheduler(), launch_job_monitor(), job_status(), stop_simulations(), close_windows(), release_desktop(), close_desktop().

parameters.name: Desktop properties
parameters.description: odesktop (native oDesktop), aedt_version_id, installed_versions, project_list, design_list(), personallib/syslib/userlib, logger, grpc_mode/is_grpc_api, non_graphical.

tools.example:
from ansys.aedt.core import Desktop, Hfss, Circuit

d = Desktop(version="2025.1", non_graphical=True, new_desktop=True, close_on_exit=True)
print(d.aedt_version_id, d.installed_versions)

hfss = Hfss(project="C:/work/filter.aedt", design="Filter")
cir = Circuit(design="Schematic")   # same project, same session

d.enable_autosave()
print(d.project_list, d.design_list())
d.release_desktop(close_projects=True, close_on_exit=True)
tools.notes: With new_desktop=False PyAEDT attaches to the first AEDT it finds, which is the usual way to script an open GUI session. Multiple independent sessions in one script need settings.use_multi_desktop = True. The Desktop object is what -RunScript inside AEDT already provides; there the constructor simply connects to the host process.

tools.name: Hfss constructor (project, design, solution_type, version, non_graphical, new_desktop, ...)
tools.description: Every application class shares the same constructor signature. Hfss() with no arguments connects to the active HFSS design or inserts a new one; giving a project path opens it, a design name selects or creates that design, and solution_type fixes the solver. The remaining arguments control the desktop session exactly like the Desktop class, so a one-liner can start a headless 2025 R1 session, open a project and hand back a ready object.
tools.usage:
hfss = Hfss(project=None, design=None, solution_type=None, setup=None, version=None,
            non_graphical=False, new_desktop=False, close_on_exit=False, student_version=False,
            machine="", port=0, aedt_process_id=None, remove_lock=False)

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project name (if already open), full path to an .aedt or .aedtz file, or None for the active project. A non-existing path creates a new project there.

parameters.name: design
parameters.description: Design name to activate; created if it does not exist. None uses the active design or inserts HFSSDesign1.

parameters.name: solution_type
parameters.description: "Modal", "Terminal", "Eigenmode", "Transient", "SBR+" or "Characteristic" for a new design; ignored when an existing design is selected.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: Name of the setup to treat as nominal; defaults to the first/active setup.

parameters.name: version
parameters.description: "2025.1", 2025.1 or 251; None uses the latest installed release.

parameters.name: non_graphical / new_desktop / close_on_exit / student_version / machine / port / aedt_process_id
parameters.description: Session options, identical to the Desktop class.

parameters.name: remove_lock
parameters.description: True deletes a stale .lock file before opening, useful after a crashed batch run.

tools.example:
from ansys.aedt.core import Hfss

# attach to whatever is open in the GUI
hfss = Hfss()

# headless session on a new project with a Terminal design
hfss = Hfss(project="C:/work/connector.aedt", design="Conn", solution_type="Terminal",
            version="2025.1", non_graphical=True, new_desktop=True, close_on_exit=True)
print(hfss.project_name, hfss.design_name, hfss.solution_type)

# attach to a running AEDT gRPC server on another machine
hfss = Hfss(machine="solve-node-01", port=50051, new_desktop=False)
tools.notes: Keyword names were renamed in the ansys.aedt.core generation (projectname -> project, designname -> design, specified_version -> version, aedt_process_id, etc.); old pyaedt code still runs but logs deprecation warnings. Use the object as a context manager (with Hfss(...) as hfss:) to guarantee release_desktop on exceptions.

tools.name: gRPC vs COM connection (settings.use_grpc_api, machine, port, aedt_process_id)
tools.description: Since AEDT 2022 R2 PyAEDT talks to the desktop through a gRPC server that AEDT starts on a port; before that, and optionally still on Windows, it used the COM interface through pythonnet. gRPC is what enables Linux, remote machines (machine/port arguments) and attaching by process id, and it is the default for supported versions. COM remains available for legacy 2021 R2/2022 R1 installations and for IronPython-hosted scripts.
tools.usage:
from ansys.aedt.core import settings
settings.use_grpc_api = True      # default None = automatic per version
hfss = Hfss(machine="host", port=50051)   # remote gRPC
hfss = Hfss(aedt_process_id=12345)          # attach to a running PID

parameters.name: settings.use_grpc_api
parameters.description: True forces gRPC, False forces COM, None lets PyAEDT decide (gRPC for 2022 R2 and later).

parameters.name: machine / port
parameters.description: Remote host and the gRPC port AEDT was started with (ansysedt -grpcsrv <port>).

parameters.name: aedt_process_id
parameters.description: Connects to that specific desktop process when several are running.

parameters.name: ansysedt -grpcsrv <port>
parameters.description: Command line flag that starts AEDT as a gRPC server for remote clients.

tools.example:
# Start AEDT as a server on the solve node:
#   ansysedt -grpcsrv 50051 -ng
# Then from a workstation:
from ansys.aedt.core import Hfss
hfss = Hfss(machine="solve-node-01", port=50051, new_desktop=False, version="2025.1")
print(hfss.desktop_class.is_grpc_api)
tools.notes: COM mode needs the pyaedt[dotnet] extra and only works on Windows. gRPC calls are retried automatically (settings.number_of_grpc_api_retries); a firewall between client and server must allow the chosen port. The student version supports gRPC too.

tools.name: settings (ansys.aedt.core.settings)
tools.description: A module-level singleton holding the PyAEDT session configuration: logging destinations and verbosity, error handling, gRPC vs COM, lazy loading of object lists, pandas output, the LSF scheduler launcher and the AEDT environment variables that enable beta features. Set attributes before creating the Desktop or application object; most take effect at launch time. The same options can be persisted in a pyaedt_settings.yaml file pointed to by the PYAEDT_LOCAL_SETTINGS_PATH environment variable.
tools.usage:
from ansys.aedt.core import settings
settings.<option> = value

parameters.name: enable_logger / enable_desktop_logs / enable_screen_logs / enable_file_logs
parameters.description: Where PyAEDT log lines go: Python logger, AEDT Message Manager, stdout and the log file (all default True except where noted).

parameters.name: logger_file_path / enable_global_log_file / enable_local_log_file
parameters.description: Log file location; the global file lives in the temp folder, the local one next to the project.

parameters.name: enable_debug_logger / enable_debug_methods_argument_logger / enable_debug_grpc_api_logger
parameters.description: Verbose debug streams, useful when reproducing a PyAEDT issue.

parameters.name: enable_error_handler
parameters.description: True wraps every call so exceptions are logged instead of raised; False (default) lets Python exceptions propagate.

parameters.name: release_on_exception
parameters.description: Release AEDT when an unhandled exception occurs (default True).

parameters.name: use_grpc_api / use_multi_desktop / desktop_launch_timeout / wait_for_license / skip_license_check
parameters.description: Session mechanics: transport, several desktops per script, launch timeout in seconds (120), -waitforlicense flag.

parameters.name: lazy_load / objects_lazy_load
parameters.description: Defer building the object/boundary inventories until first use; keep True on large models.

parameters.name: enable_pandas_output
parameters.description: Return SolutionData tables as pandas DataFrames.

parameters.name: use_lsf_scheduler / lsf_queue / num_cores / lsf_ram / lsf_timeout / lsf_aedt_command
parameters.description: Launch the AEDT process through an LSF bsub interactive job instead of locally.

parameters.name: aedt_environment_variables
parameters.description: Dictionary of ANSYSEM_FEATURE_* variables passed to the process, e.g. to enable beta features.

tools.example:
from ansys.aedt.core import settings, Hfss

settings.enable_screen_logs = False
settings.enable_debug_logger = True
settings.logger_file_path = "C:/work/logs/pyaedt_filter.log"
settings.enable_pandas_output = True
settings.aedt_environment_variables["ANSYSEM_FEATURE_SF6694_NON_GRAPHICAL_COMMAND_EXECUTION_ENABLE"] = "1"

hfss = Hfss(version="2025.1", non_graphical=True)
data = hfss.post.get_solution_data("dB(S(1,1))")
print(data.full_matrix_real_imag[0].head())   # DataFrame because pandas output is on
tools.notes: Settings are process-global, so a library that changes them affects every subsequent PyAEDT call in the interpreter. The attribute list grows with each release; print(settings.__dict__) or the Settings user guide shows what the installed version supports.

tools.name: hfss.logger (AedtLogger)
tools.description: The per-design logger PyAEDT writes to. It fans messages out to the Python logging module, the PyAEDT log file and the AEDT Message Manager window at the project or design level, so a script's own progress lines appear next to solver messages. Use it instead of print() in scripts that will run headless or under a scheduler.
tools.usage:
hfss.logger.info(msg)
hfss.logger.warning(msg)
hfss.logger.error(msg)
hfss.logger.debug(msg)
hfss.logger.add_error_message(msg, level="Design")
hfss.logger.clear_messages(proj_name=None, des_name=None, aedt_messages=True)

parameters.name: info / warning / error / debug
parameters.description: Standard severity methods. debug lines only appear when settings.enable_debug_logger is True.

parameters.name: add_info_message / add_warning_message / add_error_message
parameters.description: Write to the AEDT Message Manager explicitly at 'Global', 'Project' or 'Design' level.

parameters.name: clear_messages
parameters.description: Empty the Message Manager for the project/design; aedt_messages=True also clears AEDT's own entries.

parameters.name: logger.messages
parameters.description: Access to the message lists collected from AEDT (design/project/global messages) for parsing solver errors.

parameters.name: reset_timer / info_timer
parameters.description: Simple elapsed-time reporting for benchmarking script sections.

tools.example:
hfss.logger.info("Building geometry for %s", hfss.design_name)
hfss.logger.reset_timer()
hfss.analyze()
hfss.logger.info_timer("Solve finished")

for msg in hfss.logger.messages.design_level:
    if "error" in msg.lower():
        hfss.logger.warning("AEDT reported: %s", msg)
tools.notes: The desktop-wide logger is hfss.desktop_class.logger. In a -ng run the Message Manager still exists internally and its content is written to the log file, which is the main diagnostic after a failed batch solve. Native equivalent: oDesktop.AddMessage(project, design, severity, text).

tools.name: hfss.autosave_enable / hfss.autosave_disable
tools.description: Toggle AEDT's project autosave from a script. Autosave is convenient interactively but costly in automation: every save of a large solved project can take minutes and it blocks the gRPC call in progress, so scripts that create hundreds of objects usually disable it at the start and save explicitly at checkpoints.
tools.usage:
hfss.autosave_disable()
hfss.autosave_enable()
# or at desktop level
hfss.desktop_class.disable_autosave()
hfss.desktop_class.enable_autosave()

parameters.name: return
parameters.description: True on success. The setting is the same one shown in Tools > Options > General Options > Project Options > Do Autosave.

tools.example:
hfss = Hfss(version="2025.1", non_graphical=True)
hfss.autosave_disable()
for i in range(200):
    hfss.modeler.create_box([i, 0, 0], [0.5, 0.5, 0.5], name=f"cell_{i}")
hfss.save_project()
hfss.autosave_enable()
tools.notes: Native calls: oDesktop.EnableAutoSave(True/False). The batch option 'Desktop/Settings/ProjectOptions/DoAutoSave'=0 does the same for a command-line run.

tools.name: hfss.insert_design
tools.description: Add a new design of the application's type (HFSS for an Hfss object) to the current project and make it active. The solution type can be fixed at creation; the name is made unique automatically. Use it to build several designs in one project from a single script, for example a unit cell and a finite array, or a feed and an SBR+ platform design.
tools.usage: new_name = hfss.insert_design(name=None, solution_type=None)

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Requested design name; if it exists an index suffix is appended. None gives HFSSDesign<n>.

parameters.name: solution_type
parameters.description: "Modal", "Terminal", "Eigenmode", "Transient", "SBR+" or "Characteristic"; None uses the application default (Modal).

parameters.name: return
parameters.description: The final design name actually assigned.

tools.example:
hfss = Hfss(project="C:/work/array.aedt")
cell = hfss.insert_design("UnitCell", solution_type="Modal")
feed = hfss.insert_design("Feed", solution_type="Terminal")
print(hfss.design_list)          # ['HFSSDesign1', 'UnitCell', 'Feed']
hfss.set_active_design(cell)
tools.notes: After insert_design the Hfss object points at the new design; keep the returned name to switch back. Native equivalent: oProject.InsertDesign("HFSS", name, "DrivenModal", ""). Other design types are inserted by instantiating the matching class (Circuit(), Maxwell3d(), Icepak()) on the same project.

tools.name: hfss.set_active_design / hfss.design_list / hfss.design_name
tools.description: Switch the Hfss object to another design of the same type in the open project and inspect what designs exist. All modeler, boundary, setup and post objects are re-bound to the newly active design, so one Python object can drive several designs sequentially without reconnecting.
tools.usage:
hfss.set_active_design(name)
names = hfss.design_list        # designs of this application type in the project
current = hfss.design_name
hfss.design_name = "NewName"   # renames the active design

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Existing design name. Designs of other types (Circuit, Maxwell) are not selectable from an Hfss object; open them with their own class.

parameters.name: design_list
parameters.description: List of design names of the current design type in the project.

parameters.name: design_type
parameters.description: String such as "HFSS" or "HFSS 3D Layout Design".

tools.example:
hfss = Hfss(project="C:/work/array.aedt")
for d in hfss.design_list:
    hfss.set_active_design(d)
    print(d, hfss.solution_type, len(hfss.modeler.object_names), hfss.setup_names)
tools.notes: Setting hfss.design_name to a new string renames the design (rename_design does the same with an optional save). Native equivalents: oProject.SetActiveDesign(name), oProject.GetTopDesignList(), oDesign.RenameDesignInstance(old, new).

tools.name: hfss.duplicate_design / hfss.rename_design / hfss.delete_design
tools.description: Copy the active design under a new name (geometry, boundaries, setups and optionally results), rename it, or remove a design from the project. duplicate_design is the scripted form of right-click > Copy / Paste and is the standard way to create variants for a design comparison or to freeze a validated baseline before an optimisation.
tools.usage:
hfss.duplicate_design(name, save_after_duplicate=True)
hfss.rename_design(name, save=False)
hfss.delete_design(name=None, fallback_design=None)

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: New design name for duplicate/rename, or the design to delete (None = active design).

parameters.name: save_after_duplicate
parameters.description: Save the project once the copy exists (default True).

parameters.name: fallback_design
parameters.description: Design to activate after deleting the current one; PyAEDT needs a valid active design to keep working.

tools.example:
hfss = Hfss(project="C:/work/patch.aedt", design="Patch")
hfss.duplicate_design("Patch_thick_substrate")
hfss["h"] = "3.175mm"          # edit the copy
hfss.analyze()
hfss.set_active_design("Patch")
hfss.delete_design("Scratch", fallback_design="Patch")
tools.notes: duplicate_design activates the copy. Deleting the only design of a project leaves the Hfss object unusable until insert_design is called. Native equivalents: oProject.CopyDesign(name) + oProject.Paste(), oDesign.RenameDesignInstance, oProject.DeleteDesign(name).

tools.name: hfss.copy_design_from / hfss.copy_solid_bodies_from
tools.description: Bring content in from another project or design. copy_design_from copies a whole design out of another .aedt file into the active project; copy_solid_bodies_from copies the geometry (solids, optionally sheets and 3D components) of another open design into the current one, which is how a thermal Icepak design or an SBR+ platform design is seeded from the HFSS model without re-importing CAD.
tools.usage:
hfss.copy_design_from(project, design, save_project=True, set_active_design=True)
hfss.copy_solid_bodies_from(design, assignment=None, no_vacuum=True, no_pec=True, include_sheets=False)

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Full path of the source .aedt file for copy_design_from.

parameters.name: design
parameters.description: Source design name (copy_design_from) or the source application object, e.g. another Hfss or Hfss3dLayout instance (copy_solid_bodies_from).

parameters.name: assignment
parameters.description: List of object or 3D-component names to copy; None copies everything.

parameters.name: no_vacuum / no_pec
parameters.description: Skip vacuum objects and PEC objects, which are usually air regions and idealised conductors not wanted in a thermal or ray-tracing target.

parameters.name: include_sheets
parameters.description: Also copy sheet objects (port sheets, radiation sheets).

tools.example:
from ansys.aedt.core import Hfss, Icepak
hfss = Hfss(project="C:/work/amplifier.aedt", design="RF")
ipk = Icepak(design="Thermal")             # same project
ipk.copy_solid_bodies_from(hfss, no_vacuum=True, no_pec=False)
ipk.assign_em_losses(assignment=ipk.modeler.solid_names, design="RF", setup="Setup1", sweep="LastAdaptive")

# copy a validated design out of a library project
hfss.copy_design_from("C:/lib/feeds.aedt", "CoaxFeed")
tools.notes: copy_solid_bodies_from uses the clipboard (oEditor.Copy/Paste) so object names may receive suffixes when they clash. Materials travel with the objects. For layout designs the source must be an Hfss3dLayout object and the 3D translation is performed by AEDT on paste.

tools.name: hfss.load_project / hfss.create_new_project / hfss.project_file
tools.description: Open a second project into the running session and rebind the object to it, or create an empty new project. project_file, project_path and project_name report where the active project lives, which scripts use to build result paths next to the .aedt. These are the object-level equivalents of File > Open / New after the desktop is already up.
tools.usage:
hfss.load_project(file_name, design=None, close_active=False, set_active=True)
hfss.create_new_project(name)
hfss.project_file      # full path of the .aedt
hfss.project_path      # directory
hfss.project_name      # name without extension

parameters.name: file_name
parameters.description: Path to an .aedt or .aedtz archive; archives are extracted next to themselves before opening.

parameters.name: design
parameters.description: Design to activate after loading; None takes the first design of the application type.

parameters.name: close_active
parameters.description: Close the previously active project when the new one is loaded.

parameters.name: set_active
parameters.description: Make the loaded project the active one in the desktop (default True).

tools.example:
hfss = Hfss(version="2025.1", non_graphical=True)
hfss.load_project("C:/work/feed.aedt", design="Coax")
print(hfss.project_file)
out = os.path.join(hfss.project_path, hfss.project_name + "_S.s2p")
hfss.export_touchstone(output_file=out)
hfss.create_new_project("scratch")
tools.notes: Opening a project that is locked by another session fails unless remove_lock=True was given at construction or the .lock file is removed manually. Native equivalents: oDesktop.OpenProject(path), oDesktop.NewProject(), oProject.GetPath()/GetName().

tools.name: hfss.archive_project / hfss.copy_project / hfss.delete_project / hfss.clean_proj_folder
tools.description: Project housekeeping from a script: archive writes an .aedtz containing the project and optionally results and external files (File > Archive), copy_project saves a renamed copy elsewhere, delete_project closes and removes a project, and clean_proj_folder deletes the .aedtresults tree to reclaim disk space before archiving or committing a model.
tools.usage:
hfss.archive_project(project_path=None, include_external_files=True, include_results_file=True,
                     additional_file_lists=None, notes="")
hfss.copy_project(destination, name)
hfss.delete_project(name)
hfss.clean_proj_folder(directory=None, name=None)

parameters.name: project_path
parameters.description: Target .aedtz path; None writes next to the project.

parameters.name: include_results_file / include_external_files
parameters.description: Whether solved data and linked files (Touchstone, CAD, datasets) go into the archive.

parameters.name: additional_file_lists
parameters.description: Extra files to bundle, e.g. the generating Python script.

parameters.name: destination / name
parameters.description: Folder and new project name for copy_project.

tools.example:
hfss.analyze()
hfss.save_project()
hfss.archive_project("C:/deliver/filter_v3.aedtz", include_results_file=True,
                     additional_file_lists=["C:/work/build_filter.py"], notes="release candidate")
hfss.copy_project("C:/backup", "filter_backup")
hfss.clean_proj_folder()      # drops .aedtresults of the current project
tools.notes: An archive without results is small and is what support normally asks for; results can be regenerated. clean_proj_folder on an open project invalidates all reports until the next solve. Native: oProject.SaveAs, the Archive dialog has no simple single call.

tools.name: hfss.solution_type (property setter)
tools.description: Read or change the solver of the active design. Assigning a new value switches an existing design between Modal, Terminal, Eigenmode, Transient, SBR+ and Characteristic Mode, mirroring HFSS > Solution Type in the GUI. Switching converts what it can (ports become terminals or vice versa) and drops setups that no longer apply, so do it before boundaries and setups are created.
tools.usage:
hfss.solution_type                 # e.g. 'Modal'
hfss.solution_type = "Terminal"     # switch the design
hfss.hybrid = True                  # enable hybrid FEM-IE/SBR+ regions
hfss.composite = True               # composite (auto-open) variant

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: "Modal", "Terminal", "Eigenmode", "Transient", "SBR+", "Characteristic" (PyAEDT also accepts the native strings such as "HFSS Terminal Network").

parameters.name: hfss.hybrid
parameters.description: Boolean flag that turns on the hybrid (IE/PO/SBR+) capability of a Driven design.

parameters.name: hfss.composite
parameters.description: Boolean flag for the composite excitation/auto-open form of the solution type.

tools.example:
hfss = Hfss(design="Connector")
print(hfss.solution_type)          # Modal
hfss.solution_type = "Terminal"
hfss.hybrid = True
hfss.assign_hybrid_region("Radome", hybrid_region="IE")
tools.notes: Native: oDesign.SetSolutionType("HFSS Terminal Network", ["NAME:Options", "EnableAutoOpen:=", False]). Terminal designs need a reference conductor for every port; converting a Modal design with wave ports but no terminals produces ports without terminals that must be fixed with auto-identify.

tools.name: hfss.change_design_settings / hfss.change_material_override / hfss.change_automatically_use_causal_materials
tools.description: Script the HFSS > Design Settings dialog. change_design_settings takes a dictionary of the native setting names (material override, lossy dielectric calculation, advanced DC extrapolation, port validation level, export after simulation) and the two convenience methods flip the most common switches: allowing a material override so overlapping objects do not fail validation, and automatically replacing frequency-independent dielectrics by causal (Djordjevic-Sarkar) models for broadband sweeps.
tools.usage:
hfss.change_design_settings(settings)          # dict of native names -> values
hfss.change_material_override(material_override=True)
hfss.change_automatically_use_causal_materials(lossy_dielectric=True)
hfss.change_validation_settings(entity_check_level="Strict", ignore_unclassified=False, skip_intersections=False)

parameters.name: settings
parameters.description: Keys as in the Design Settings Data array: "Allow Material Override", "Calculate Lossy Dielectrics", "Use Advanced DC Extrapolation", "Use Power S", "Export After Simulation", "Port Validation Settings" ("Standard"/"Extended"), "Maximum Number of Frequencies for Broadband Adapt".

parameters.name: entity_check_level
parameters.description: "Strict", "Basic" or "None" for the model validation entity check.

parameters.name: ignore_unclassified
parameters.description: Skip unclassified objects during validation instead of failing.

tools.example:
hfss.change_material_override(True)
hfss.change_automatically_use_causal_materials(True)
hfss.change_design_settings({"Use Advanced DC Extrapolation": True,
                             "Port Validation Settings": "Extended"})
ok = hfss.validate_full_design()
tools.notes: Native call: oDesign.SetDesignSettings(["NAME:Design Settings Data", ...], ["NAME:Model Validation Settings", ...]). Material override lets the later object in the history tree win inside an intersection; it hides modelling errors, so use it deliberately.

tools.name: hfss.set_auto_open
tools.description: Enable or disable Auto Open Region for the design and choose the truncation it uses. With auto open switched on, HFSS surrounds the model with an automatically sized air region terminated by a radiation boundary, PML or FE-BI at solve time, so no explicit air box or boundary needs to be drawn; this is the scripted form of the Auto Open option in HFSS > Solution Type / Design Settings.
tools.usage: hfss.set_auto_open(enable=True, opening_type="Radiation")

parameters.name: enable
parameters.description: True switches auto-open on, False returns to manual regions and boundaries.

parameters.name: opening_type
parameters.description: "Radiation", "FEBI" or "PML" - which absorbing termination is generated on the automatic region.

tools.example:
hfss = Hfss(solution_type="Terminal")
hfss.set_auto_open(True, "PML")
# no create_open_region / create_region needed; solve directly
hfss.create_setup("Setup1", Frequency="5GHz")
hfss.analyze()
tools.notes: Native: oDesign.SetSolutionType(<type>, ["NAME:Options", "EnableAutoOpen:=", True, "ModelExteriorAsIE:=", "PML"]). Auto open is not available in Eigenmode; create_open_region remains the explicit alternative when the air padding must be controlled.

tools.name: hfss.validate_full_design / hfss.validate_simple
tools.description: Run the HFSS validation check (Validate button) from a script and get the result back. validate_simple returns only pass/fail and writes the log; validate_full_design also parses the log, counts errors and warnings, optionally checks that every port has a valid excitation and returns the message lists so a build script can stop before a doomed solve.
tools.usage:
ok = hfss.validate_simple(log_file=None)
messages, ok = hfss.validate_full_design(name=None, output_dir=None, ports=None)

parameters.name: log_file
parameters.description: Path for the validation log; None uses the working directory.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Design to validate; None is the active design.

parameters.name: ports
parameters.description: Expected number of excitations; validation fails if the design has fewer.

parameters.name: return
parameters.description: validate_full_design returns (list_of_messages, bool); the messages include validation warnings and errors from the Message Manager.

tools.notes: Validation catches missing materials, overlapping objects without material override, ports without integration lines in Modal designs and boundaries on deleted faces. It does not check mesh feasibility; only the first adaptive pass does. Native: oDesign.ValidateDesign() plus reading the Message Manager.

tools.name: hfss.variable_manager.set_variable
tools.description: The full-featured way to create or edit design and project variables. The item syntax hfss["w"] = "1mm" covers value setting; set_variable adds the flags shown in the Properties window - read-only, hidden, description, whether the variable participates in solution indexing (sweep), post-processing variables that do not invalidate results - and can set a list of variables in one call.
tools.usage:
hfss.variable_manager.set_variable(name, expression=None, read_only=False, hidden=False,
                                   description=None, sweep=True, overwrite=True,
                                   is_post_processing=False, circuit_parameter=True)

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Variable name or list of names. A leading $ makes it a project variable.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: AEDT expression string with units, e.g. "3*cos(34deg)" or "patch_w/2"; a plain number is taken without units.

parameters.name: read_only / hidden / description
parameters.description: Properties-window flags of the variable.

parameters.name: sweep
parameters.description: True lets the variable index solutions (default). False marks it non-sweepable, which keeps it out of Optimetrics.

parameters.name: is_post_processing
parameters.description: True creates a post-processing variable: changing it does not invalidate solved results and it can be tuned in reports.

parameters.name: overwrite
parameters.description: False leaves an existing variable untouched.

tools.example:
vm = hfss.variable_manager
vm.set_variable("patch_w", "38mm", description="patch width")
vm.set_variable("$sub_h", "1.575mm")                      # project variable
vm.set_variable("scan_phase", "0deg", is_post_processing=True)
vm.set_variable(["l1", "l2"], ["10mm", "12mm"], read_only=[False, True])
print(vm.design_variable_names, vm.project_variable_names)
tools.notes: Native equivalent: oDesign.ChangeProperty with LocalVariableTab (design) or oProject.ChangeProperty with ProjectVariableTab (project) and the NewProps array containing PropType 'VariableProp' or 'PostProcessingVariableProp'. Units are stored with the value; a variable created without units is dimensionless.

tools.name: hfss.evaluate_expression / hfss.get_evaluated_value / Quantity
tools.description: Turn AEDT expressions into numbers. evaluate_expression asks the desktop to evaluate any valid expression string (variables, functions, units) and returns a float in SI; get_evaluated_value returns the evaluated value of a named variable, optionally in requested units. The Quantity class in ansys.aedt.core.generic.numbers_utils does unit-aware arithmetic on the Python side without a desktop round-trip.
tools.usage:
val = hfss.evaluate_expression(expression)
val = hfss.get_evaluated_value(name, units=None)
from ansys.aedt.core.generic.numbers_utils import Quantity
q = Quantity(1, "GHz"); q2 = q + "1MHz"; q.to("MHz")

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: Any AEDT expression, e.g. "$sub_h*2 + 1mm" or "if(w>1mm, 1, 0)".

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Variable name; get_evaluated_value resolves dependencies and returns the value in SI unless units is given.

parameters.name: Quantity(value, unit)
parameters.description: Supports +, -, *, /, comparison, .to(unit), .unit and .value; unit strings follow AEDT conventions (mm, mil, GHz, deg).

tools.example:
hfss["$sub_h"] = "1.575mm"
hfss["gap"] = "$sub_h/4 + 0.1mm"
print(hfss.evaluate_expression("gap*2"))        # 0.0009875 (metres)
print(hfss.get_evaluated_value("gap", units="mm"))

from ansys.aedt.core.generic.numbers_utils import Quantity
f0 = Quantity(2.45, "GHz")
lam = Quantity(299792458, "m") / f0.to("Hz").value
print(lam.to("mm"))
tools.notes: evaluate_expression needs a live design because it uses AEDT's own evaluator (same as the Properties window). Expressions may use if(), pwl(dataset, x), sin/cos/tan, sqrt, abs, min/max, and project variables prefixed with $.

tools.name: hfss.delete_variable / hfss.delete_unused_variables / hfss.hidden_variable / hfss.read_only_variable
tools.description: Variable lifecycle helpers: delete a single design or project variable, sweep out every variable that no geometry, boundary or setup references, and toggle the hidden / read-only flags that control what a user of the design can see or edit in the Properties window. Cleaning unused variables before an Optimetrics study keeps the variable list, the solution index and the parametric table small.
tools.usage:
hfss.delete_variable(name)
hfss.delete_unused_variables()
hfss.hidden_variable(name, value=True)
hfss.read_only_variable(name, value=True)
hfss.variable_manager.is_used(name)

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Variable name, with $ for project scope.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: True hides / locks the variable, False shows / unlocks it.

parameters.name: is_used
parameters.description: Reports whether any expression in the design depends on the variable.

tools.notes: Deleting a variable that is still referenced fails (AEDT refuses); check is_used first. Hidden variables are still usable in expressions and Optimetrics. Native: oDesign.ChangeProperty with DeletedProps / ChangedProps arrays.

tools.name: VariableManager.variables / design_variables / project_variables / independent_variables / dependent_variables
tools.description: Dictionaries of Variable objects describing everything defined in the project and design, split by scope (design vs project) and by nature (independent values vs dependent expressions), plus post_processing_variables. Each Variable exposes .expression, .value (numeric in SI), .units, .evaluated_value and .numeric_value, so a script can audit, log or export the whole parameter space without parsing the Properties window.
tools.usage:
vm = hfss.variable_manager
vm.variables                    # all
vm.design_variables / vm.project_variables
vm.independent_variables / vm.dependent_variables
vm.independent_design_variable_names / vm.dependent_project_variable_names
vm["patch_w"].expression / .value / .units / .evaluated_value

parameters.name: Variable.expression
parameters.description: The string as typed, e.g. "2*$sub_h"; assignable to change the definition.

parameters.name: Variable.value / numeric_value
parameters.description: Evaluated number in SI units / in the variable's own units.

parameters.name: Variable.units
parameters.description: Unit string, empty for dimensionless.

parameters.name: *_names lists
parameters.description: Name-only lists for quick membership tests and iteration.

tools.example:
vm = hfss.variable_manager
for name, var in vm.independent_design_variables.items():
    print(f"{name} = {var.expression}  ({var.numeric_value} {var.units})")
vm["patch_l"].expression = "patch_w*0.76"
print(vm.dependent_design_variable_names)
tools.notes: Native: oDesign.GetVariables()/GetVariableValue(name) and oProject.GetVariables() return only names and expression strings; PyAEDT evaluates them. Post-processing variables live in vm.post_processing_variables.

tools.name: hfss.create_dataset / create_dataset1d_design / create_dataset1d_project
tools.description: Create a project or design dataset (a tabulated x-y or x-y-z-v function) directly from Python lists. Datasets are referenced in expressions through pwl(dsname, x) and in materials for frequency- or temperature-dependent properties, and 3D datasets feed thermal modifiers and spatially varying loads. The dataset is created in the project tree exactly as with Project > Datasets > Add.
tools.usage:
ds = hfss.create_dataset(name, x, y, z=None, v=None, is_project_dataset=True,
                         x_unit="", y_unit="", z_unit="", v_unit="", sort=True)
ds = hfss.create_dataset1d_design(name, x, y, x_unit="", y_unit="", sort=True)
ds = hfss.create_dataset1d_project(name, x, y, x_unit="", y_unit="", sort=True)
ds = hfss.create_dataset3d(name, x, y, z=None, v=None, ...)

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Dataset name; project datasets are addressed as $name in expressions.

parameters.name: x, y (z, v)
parameters.description: Equal-length lists of numbers; sorted by x when sort=True.

parameters.name: x_unit / y_unit
parameters.description: Units attached to the columns, e.g. "GHz" and "" for a unitless permittivity.

parameters.name: is_project_dataset
parameters.description: True makes it a project dataset visible to all designs.

parameters.name: return
parameters.description: A DataSet object with .name, .x, .y, .update(), .delete() and .add_point().

tools.example:
freqs = [1, 2, 4, 8, 12]
er    = [4.4, 4.35, 4.3, 4.22, 4.15]
ds = hfss.create_dataset("$er_fr4", freqs, er, x_unit="GHz", is_project_dataset=True)
hfss["er_at_f0"] = "pwl($er_fr4, 2.45GHz)"
print(hfss.project_datasets.keys(), ds.x)
tools.notes: pwl() interpolates linearly and holds the end values outside the range. Native: oProject.AddDataset(["NAME:$er_fr4", ["NAME:Coordinates", ["NAME:Coordinate", "X:=", 1, "Y:=", 4.4], ...]]) / oDesign.AddDataset. Design datasets do not need the $ prefix.

tools.name: hfss.import_dataset1d / hfss.import_dataset3d / hfss.dataset_exists / hfss.design_datasets
tools.description: Load datasets from tab- or comma-separated files (the same files the Datasets dialog imports), test for existence and enumerate the datasets of the project and design. Measured material data, antenna weights or a temperature profile exported from another tool are brought in this way and then used through pwl() or as material property datasets.
tools.usage:
ds = hfss.import_dataset1d(input_file, name=None, is_project_dataset=True, sort=True)
ds = hfss.import_dataset3d(input_file, xlist=None, ylist=None, zlist=None, vlist=None, is_project_dataset=True)
hfss.dataset_exists(name, is_project=True)
hfss.project_datasets   # dict name -> DataSet
hfss.design_datasets

parameters.name: input_file
parameters.description: Two-column (1D) or four-column (3D) text file; a header line with units is honoured.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Dataset name; defaults to the file name without extension.

parameters.name: is_project_dataset
parameters.description: Scope of the dataset.

tools.notes: Native: oProject.ImportDataset(path). Datasets are stored inside the .aedt, not linked, so re-import after the source file changes. DataSet.update() pushes edited x/y lists back to AEDT.

tools.name: hfss.create_output_variable / hfss.get_output_variable / hfss.output_variables
tools.description: Define output variables - named report expressions such as dB(S(1,1)) at a frequency or max gain - that Optimetrics goals, cost functions and other reports can reference, then read their evaluated values. The scripted form of Results > Output Variables, and the cleanest way to hand a scalar figure of merit from a solved design back to Python.
tools.usage:
hfss.create_output_variable(variable, expression, solution=None, context=None, is_differential=False)
value = hfss.get_output_variable(variable, solution=None)
hfss.output_variables       # list of names

parameters.name: variable
parameters.description: Output variable name.

parameters.name: expression
parameters.description: Report expression, e.g. "dB(S(1,1))", "max(dB(GainTotal))" or "abs(Z(1,1))".

parameters.name: solution
parameters.description: "Setup1 : LastAdaptive" or "Setup1 : Sweep1"; None takes the first available solution.

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: Report context such as an infinite sphere name for far-field expressions.

parameters.name: is_differential
parameters.description: True for differential-pair S-parameters in Circuit / 3D Layout designs.

tools.example:
hfss.create_output_variable("RL_2p45", "dB(S(1,1))", solution="Setup1 : Sweep1")
hfss.create_output_variable("PeakGain", "max(dB(GainTotal))", solution="Setup1 : LastAdaptive", context="3D")
hfss.analyze()
print(hfss.output_variables, hfss.get_output_variable("PeakGain"))
tools.notes: Native: oModule = oDesign.GetModule("OutputVariable"); oModule.CreateOutputVariable(name, expr, solution, reportType, contextArray) and oDesign.GetOutputVariableValue(name, intrinsicVariation, solution, reportType, context). An output variable with a frequency-dependent expression needs the frequency fixed through the intrinsic variation when evaluated.

tools.name: hfss.materials (Materials): material_keys, exists_material, remove_material, conductors, dielectrics
tools.description: The Materials object is the project material database: a dictionary of Material objects for every material already used or added in the project, with lookups into the system library. It answers whether a name exists (case-insensitively), classifies materials as conductors or dielectrics using the conductivity threshold, removes unused project materials and gives access to the native definition and material managers.
tools.usage:
mats = hfss.materials
mats["copper"]                      # Material object (loads from library on first access)
mats.material_keys                  # dict of project materials
mats.exists_material(name)          # bool, library included
mats.conductors / mats.dielectrics / mats.gases / mats.liquids
mats.remove_material(material, library="Project")
mats.get_used_project_material_names()
mats.mat_names_aedt / mats.mat_names_aedt_lower

parameters.name: material_keys
parameters.description: Lower-case name -> Material for materials present in the project (system-library materials are added on first use).

parameters.name: exists_material
parameters.description: Checks project and AEDT library definitions; the old name checkifmaterialexists is deprecated.

parameters.name: conductors / dielectrics
parameters.description: Name lists split by conductivity threshold (hfss.set_material_threshold changes the threshold, default 1e5 S/m).

parameters.name: remove_material
parameters.description: Deletes a project-level material; library materials cannot be removed.

tools.notes: Material names with spaces and (tm) must be given exactly as in the library; lookups are case-insensitive. Native managers: hfss.odefinition_manager (AddMaterial, DoesMaterialExist, EditMaterial) and hfss.omaterial_manager.

tools.name: Material object properties (permittivity, permeability, conductivity, dielectric_loss_tangent, thermal_conductivity, mass_density, ...)
tools.description: Each Material returned by hfss.materials exposes its properties as MatProperty objects whose .value can be a number, an expression, a dataset reference or an anisotropic 3-component list, and which carry an optional thermal modifier. Setting .value edits the material in place and pushes it to AEDT (update() re-syncs everything), so a new material is defined by add_material followed by property assignments.
tools.usage:
m = hfss.materials.add_material(name, properties=None)
m.permittivity.value = 4.4
m.dielectric_loss_tangent.value = 0.02
m.conductivity.value = 5.8e7
m.permeability.value = [1, 1, 1.2]        # anisotropic diagonal
m.magnetic_loss_tangent.value = 0
m.thermal_conductivity.value = 0.3
m.mass_density.value = 1850
m.specific_heat.value = 1000
m.material_appearance = [255, 128, 0]
m.coordinate_system = "Cartesian"
m.update()

parameters.name: Electromagnetic
parameters.description: permittivity, permeability, conductivity, dielectric_loss_tangent, magnetic_loss_tangent, magnetic_coercivity (+ set_magnetic_coercivity), core-loss models for Maxwell.

parameters.name: Thermal / mechanical
parameters.description: thermal_conductivity, mass_density, specific_heat, thermal_expansion_coefficient, youngs_modulus, poissons_ratio, diffusivity, viscosity, molecular_mass.

parameters.name: MatProperty.thermalmodifier
parameters.description: Expression in Temp, e.g. "1+0.002*(Temp-22)", or a dataset; the thermal modifier of the property.

parameters.name: MatProperty.type
parameters.description: "simple", "anisotropic", "tensor" or "nonlinear"; setting a 3-element list switches to anisotropic.

parameters.name: is_conductor() / is_dielectric()
parameters.description: Classification against the conductivity threshold.

tools.example:
fr4 = hfss.materials.add_material("FR4_custom")
fr4.permittivity.value = 4.4
fr4.dielectric_loss_tangent.value = 0.02
fr4.thermal_conductivity.value = 0.3
fr4.permittivity.thermalmodifier = "1 + 0.0004*(Temp-22)"
fr4.material_appearance = [0, 128, 0]
fr4.update()

cu = hfss.materials.duplicate_material("copper", "copper_rough")
cu.conductivity.value = 4.1e7
hfss.assign_material("Trace", "copper_rough")
tools.notes: Native: oDefinitionManager.AddMaterial(["NAME:FR4_custom", "CoordinateSystemType:=", "Cartesian", "permittivity:=", "4.4", "dielectric_loss_tangent:=", "0.02"]). Editing a library material through PyAEDT creates a project copy with the same name rather than altering SysLib.

tools.name: Material.set_djordjevic_sarkar_model
tools.description: Give a dielectric a causal, frequency-dependent permittivity and loss tangent using the Djordjevic-Sarkar (wideband Debye) model, the same option as Set Frequency Dependency > Djordjevic-Sarkar in the material editor. Supply the measured Dk and Df at a reference frequency and the model extrapolates consistently across a broadband sweep, which is required for accurate time-domain and TDR results and avoids passivity/causality warnings on Touchstone export.
tools.usage: material.set_djordjevic_sarkar_model(dk=4, df=0.02, i_freq=1e9, sigma_dc=1e-12, freq_hi=159154943091.895)

parameters.name: dk
parameters.description: Relative permittivity at the reference frequency.

parameters.name: df
parameters.description: Loss tangent at the reference frequency.

parameters.name: i_freq
parameters.description: Reference (input) frequency in Hz.

parameters.name: sigma_dc
parameters.description: DC conductivity of the dielectric in S/m.

parameters.name: freq_hi
parameters.description: Upper frequency of the model in Hz (default 159 GHz).

tools.example:
ro = hfss.materials.duplicate_material("Rogers RO4350B (tm)", "RO4350B_DS")
ro.set_djordjevic_sarkar_model(dk=3.66, df=0.0037, i_freq=10e9, sigma_dc=1e-12)
hfss.assign_material(["Sub"], "RO4350B_DS")
tools.notes: Alternatively, hfss.change_automatically_use_causal_materials(True) makes HFSS apply a causal model to every constant-property dielectric at solve time. Debye / multipole Debye models can be entered through the material's frequency-dependency dialog or by attaching datasets to permittivity and loss tangent.

tools.name: Materials.duplicate_material / Materials.add_material_sweep
tools.description: duplicate_material clones an existing (library or project) material under a new name so it can be edited without touching the original; add_material_sweep builds a sweep material whose properties are indexed by a design variable, so an Optimetrics parametric sweep can step through a list of candidate materials as if they were a single material with a variable index.
tools.usage:
new = hfss.materials.duplicate_material(material, name=None, properties=None)
sweep = hfss.materials.add_material_sweep(assignment, name)

parameters.name: material
parameters.description: Source material name for duplicate_material.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: New material name; duplicate_material appends _clone when omitted.

parameters.name: properties
parameters.description: Optional list of property names to copy; default copies everything.

parameters.name: assignment
parameters.description: List of material names that make up the sweep material (add_material_sweep).

parameters.name: return
parameters.description: Material object; the sweep material creates a variable named $ID<name> (project) that selects the active member.

tools.example:
sw = hfss.materials.add_material_sweep(["Rogers RO4003C (tm)", "Rogers RO4350B (tm)", "FR4_epoxy"], "sub_sweep")
hfss.assign_material("Sub", "sub_sweep")
param = hfss.parametrics.add("$IDsub_sweep", 0, 2, 1, "LinearStep")
param.analyze()
tools.notes: Sweep materials use datasets internally, so every property becomes pwl(dataset, $ID...); they are meant for parametric studies, not for final designs. duplicate_material of a library material always lands in the project library.

tools.name: Materials.import_materials_from_file / export_materials_to_file / import_materials_from_excel / import_materials_from_workbench
tools.description: Move material definitions between projects and tools. import_materials_from_file reads an AEDT .amat library or a PyAEDT JSON/TOML file, export_materials_to_file writes the project materials to JSON/TOML for version control, import_materials_from_excel builds materials from a spreadsheet with one property per column, and import_materials_from_workbench reads an Engineering Data XML export from Ansys Workbench.
tools.usage:
hfss.materials.import_materials_from_file(input_file=None, **kwargs)
hfss.materials.export_materials_to_file(output_file)
hfss.materials.import_materials_from_excel(input_file)
hfss.materials.import_materials_from_workbench(input_file, name_suffix="_wb")

parameters.name: input_file
parameters.description: .amat, .json or .toml (import), .csv/.xlsx (excel import), Engineering Data .xml (workbench).

parameters.name: output_file
parameters.description: Destination .json or .toml; the file lists every material with its properties and thermal modifiers.

parameters.name: return
parameters.description: List of created material names (imports) or True (export).

tools.example:
names = hfss.materials.import_materials_from_file("C:/lib/company_materials.amat")
print(names)
hfss.materials.export_materials_to_file("C:/work/project_materials.json")
hfss.materials.import_materials_from_excel("C:/lib/laminates.xlsx")
tools.notes: The .amat format is the one Tools > Edit Libraries > Materials exports; put shared .amat files in the UserLib or PersonalLib folder to make them visible in the Select Definition dialog of every project. JSON/TOML files are PyAEDT-specific.

tools.name: hfss.assign_material / hfss.get_object_material_properties / hfss.get_all_conductors_names / hfss.get_all_dielectrics_names
tools.description: Assign a material to one or more objects after creation and query what the model is made of. get_object_material_properties returns the requested property values for a list of objects, and the two name helpers list every conductor and dielectric object in the design - the usual input for finite-conductivity, skin-depth mesh and loss-mapping operations.
tools.usage:
hfss.assign_material(assignment, material)
props = hfss.get_object_material_properties(assignment=None, prop_names=None)
hfss.get_all_conductors_names()
hfss.get_all_dielectrics_names()
hfss.modeler.get_objects_by_material(material)

parameters.name: assignment
parameters.description: Object name, list of names, or Object3d handles.

parameters.name: material
parameters.description: Existing material name; a missing name makes the call fail, so check with materials.exists_material first.

parameters.name: prop_names
parameters.description: e.g. ["permittivity", "conductivity"]; None returns all properties.

tools.example:
hfss.assign_material(["Patch", "Gnd"], "copper")
cond = hfss.get_all_conductors_names()
hfss.mesh.assign_skin_depth(cond, skin_depth="2um", layers_number=2)
print(hfss.get_object_material_properties(["Sub"], ["permittivity", "dielectric_loss_tangent"]))
tools.notes: Object3d.material_name = "copper" is the per-object equivalent. Native: oEditor.AssignMaterial(["NAME:Selections", "Selections:=", "Patch,Gnd"], ["NAME:Attributes", "MaterialValue:=", "\"copper\"", "SolveInside:=", False]). Assigning a good conductor sets Solve Inside off automatically.

tools.name: hfss.working_directory / results_directory / temp_directory / set_temporary_directory
tools.description: Paths a script needs for input and output. working_directory is a per-design folder that PyAEDT creates under the project results folder and uses as the default target for exports (Touchstone, field files, images); results_directory is the .aedtresults tree; temp_directory is AEDT's temp folder, and set_temporary_directory moves it, which matters on clusters where /tmp is small or slow.
tools.usage:
hfss.working_directory      # <project>.aedtresults/<design>.results or project folder
hfss.results_directory      # <project>.aedtresults
hfss.temp_directory
hfss.set_temporary_directory(path)
hfss.toolkit_directory       # per-project folder for PyAEDT toolkit data

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Existing directory used for solver scratch files (set through the Desktop/TempDirectory registry setting).

tools.example:
import os
hfss.set_temporary_directory("D:/scratch/aedt_tmp")
out = os.path.join(hfss.working_directory, "S_params.s2p")
hfss.export_touchstone(output_file=out)
print(os.listdir(hfss.results_directory))
tools.notes: The temp directory can also be set for a batch run with -batchoptions "'TempDirectory'='/scratch/tmp'". Exports default to working_directory when no path is given, so always print or log it in headless runs.

tools.name: hfss.odesign / hfss.oproject / hfss.odesktop / hfss.oeditor / hfss.get_module
tools.description: The native AEDT automation objects behind a PyAEDT application: exactly the oDesktop, oProject, oDesign and oEditor of a recorded script, plus get_module("BoundarySetup") for any module. Use them to call something PyAEDT has not wrapped yet, pasting the argument array from Tools > Record Script To File unchanged. Convenience properties exist for every module: oboundary, omeshmodule (as oanalysis for setups), oreportsetup, ofieldsreporter, oradfield, ooptimetrics, osolution, odefinition_manager, omaterial_manager, ooutput_variable.
tools.usage:
hfss.odesktop / hfss.oproject / hfss.odesign / hfss.oeditor
mod = hfss.get_module("BoundarySetup")      # any module name accepted by oDesign.GetModule
hfss.oboundary, hfss.oanalysis, hfss.omeshmodule, hfss.oreportsetup, hfss.ofieldsreporter,
hfss.oradfield, hfss.ooptimetrics, hfss.osolution, hfss.odefinition_manager

parameters.name: module name
parameters.description: "BoundarySetup", "MeshSetup", "AnalysisSetup", "ReportSetup", "FieldsReporter", "RadField", "Optimetrics", "Solutions", "OutputVariable", "ModelSetup".

tools.example:
# a call recorded in the GUI, replayed through PyAEDT
oModule = hfss.get_module("BoundarySetup")
oModule.AssignLumpedRLC(["NAME:LumpRLC1", "Objects:=", ["RLCSheet"],
    ["NAME:CurrentLine", "Start:=", ["0mm", "0mm", "0mm"], "End:=", ["0mm", "1mm", "0mm"]],
    "RLC Type:=", "Parallel", "UseResist:=", True, "Resistance:=", "50ohm",
    "UseInduct:=", False, "UseCap:=", True, "Capacitance:=", "1pF"])

print(hfss.oeditor.GetModelBoundingBox())
hfss.odesktop.AddMessage(hfss.project_name, hfss.design_name, 0, "native call done")
tools.notes: Native objects returned through gRPC accept Python lists for arrays and True/False for booleans; VBScript-style Array(...) from old .vbs scripts must be converted. After native edits, PyAEDT caches (boundaries, setups, object lists) may be stale - call the relevant refresh (e.g. hfss.modeler.refresh_all_ids()).

tools.name: hfss.get_oo_object / get_oo_property_value / set_oo_property_value / get_oo_name / get_oo_properties
tools.description: Wrappers for the object-oriented ChildObject API that AEDT 2020 R2+ exposes on every design item (boundaries, setups, sweeps, reports, mesh operations). Instead of re-sending a whole argument array, a script fetches the child by path, lists its properties and reads or sets a single one - the mechanism PyAEDT itself uses for .props updates and the fastest way to tweak one option of an existing setup or boundary.
tools.usage:
obj = hfss.get_oo_object(aedt_object, object_name)
names = hfss.get_oo_name(aedt_object, object_name=None)
props = hfss.get_oo_properties(aedt_object, object_name=None)
val = hfss.get_oo_property_value(aedt_object, object_name, prop_name)
hfss.set_oo_property_value(aedt_object, object_name, prop_name, value)

parameters.name: aedt_object
parameters.description: Root native object, usually hfss.odesign (or hfss.oproject / hfss.oeditor).

parameters.name: object_name
parameters.description: Path of the child, e.g. "Boundaries/Port1", "AnalysisSetup/Setup1", "Mesh/Length1", "Results/S11 plot".

parameters.name: prop_name
parameters.description: Property name as shown in the Properties window, e.g. "Num Modes", "Max Delta S", "Solution Freq".

tools.example:
print(hfss.get_oo_name(hfss.odesign, "Boundaries"))            # ['Port1', 'PerfE1', ...]
print(hfss.get_oo_properties(hfss.odesign, "Boundaries/Port1"))
print(hfss.get_oo_property_value(hfss.odesign, "Boundaries/Port1", "Num Modes"))
hfss.set_oo_property_value(hfss.odesign, "AnalysisSetup/Setup1", "Max Delta S", "0.01")

# native form
child = hfss.odesign.GetChildObject("Boundaries").GetChildObject("Port1")
print(child.GetPropNames(), child.GetPropValue("Num Modes"))
tools.notes: Native ChildObject methods: GetChildNames(), GetChildObject(name), GetPropNames(), GetPropValue(name), SetPropValue(name, value), GetPropEvaluatedValue. Property names are the GUI labels and are release-dependent; list them first.

tools.name: hfss.configurations.export_config / import_config
tools.description: Serialise the non-geometric definition of a design - variables, materials, boundaries, excitations, mesh operations, setups, sweeps, Optimetrics, reports - to a JSON file and apply such a file to another design. It is PyAEDT's project template mechanism: draw or import geometry once, then stamp a validated simulation configuration on it, or diff two configurations in version control.
tools.usage:
path = hfss.configurations.export_config(config_file=None, overwrite=False)
ok = hfss.configurations.import_config(config_file, *args)
hfss.configurations.options.<flag> = True/False   # choose sections (materials, setups, boundaries, ...)
hfss.configurations.results   # validation report after import

parameters.name: config_file
parameters.description: JSON path; export defaults to the working directory.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: ConfigurationOptions with booleans such as export_materials, export_setups, export_boundaries, export_mesh_operations, export_variables, export_optimizations, import_* counterparts, unset_all()/set_all().

parameters.name: results
parameters.description: ImportResults object listing which items were applied or failed.

tools.example:
hfss.configurations.options.unset_all_export()
hfss.configurations.options.export_setups = True
hfss.configurations.options.export_boundaries = True
cfg = hfss.configurations.export_config("C:/work/filter_config.json")

other = Hfss(project="C:/work/filter_v2.aedt")
other.configurations.import_config(cfg)
print(other.configurations.results.global_import_success)
tools.notes: Boundaries are matched to geometry by object/face names and positions, so the target must use the same object names. 3D Layout has its own configuration format (h3d.configurations) and PyEDB has edb.configuration for layout-level JSON.

tools.name: hfss.export_variables_to_csv / hfss.export_design_preview_to_jpg / hfss.edit_notes
tools.description: Small documentation helpers: dump all project and design variables with their expressions and evaluated values to CSV, save a preview image of the design (the picture shown in the project manager), and write the design notes text (HFSS > Edit Notes) from a script so a generated model records how and when it was built.
tools.usage:
hfss.export_variables_to_csv(output_file, export_project=True, export_design=True)
hfss.export_design_preview_to_jpg(output_file)
hfss.edit_notes(text)

parameters.name: output_file
parameters.description: Target .csv or .jpg path.

parameters.name: export_project / export_design
parameters.description: Include project ($) and/or design variables.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: Notes string; replaces existing notes.

tools.example:
import datetime
hfss.edit_notes(f"Generated by build_filter.py on {datetime.date.today()} - PyAEDT {hfss.pyaedt_dir}")
hfss.export_variables_to_csv("C:/work/filter_vars.csv")
hfss.export_design_preview_to_jpg("C:/work/filter_preview.jpg")
tools.notes: The preview image is the low-resolution snapshot AEDT stores in the project; for a proper picture use hfss.post.export_model_picture. Notes are stored in the .aedt and visible in the Properties window of the design.

tools.name: hfss.set_license_type / set_registry_key / get_registry_key_string / get_registry_key_int / set_registry_from_file
tools.description: Read and write AEDT registry-backed preferences from a script: the HPC license mode (Pack vs Pool), arbitrary Desktop/... keys such as the project directory or autosave, and whole preference sets from an .acf/.act file exported by the HPC and Analysis Options dialog. These are the same settings -batchoptions overrides on the command line, so a script can configure a session identically to a batch job.
tools.usage:
hfss.set_license_type(license_type="Pool")            # or "Pack"
hfss.set_registry_key(key_full_name, key_value)
hfss.get_registry_key_string(key_full_name)
hfss.get_registry_key_int(key_full_name)
hfss.set_registry_from_file(registry_file, make_active=True)
hfss.set_active_dso_config_name(product_name="HFSS", config_name="Local")

parameters.name: key_full_name
parameters.description: Registry path such as "Desktop/ProjectDirectory", "Desktop/Settings/ProjectOptions/DoAutoSave", "HFSS/HPCLicenseType", "HFSS/NumCoresPerDistributedTask".

parameters.name: registry_file
parameters.description: .acf analysis configuration file; make_active selects it as the active HPC configuration.

parameters.name: config_name
parameters.description: Name of an existing HPC and Analysis Options configuration to activate for the product.

tools.example:
hfss.set_license_type("Pool")
hfss.set_registry_key("Desktop/ProjectDirectory", "D:/aedt_projects")
print(hfss.get_registry_key_string("Desktop/ProjectDirectory"))
hfss.set_registry_from_file("C:/hpc/cluster16.acf", make_active=True)
tools.notes: Native: oDesktop.SetRegistryString/SetRegistryInt, GetRegistryString/GetRegistryInt, SetActiveDSOConfigName(product, name), GetActiveDSOConfigName(product). Registry changes persist for the user beyond the session; prefer -batchoptions for one-off runs.

tools.name: generate_unique_name (ansys.aedt.core.generic.general_methods)
tools.description: Utility that appends a short random suffix to a root string, producing names that will not collide with existing objects, boundaries, setups or projects. PyAEDT uses it internally whenever a name argument is omitted; scripts use it to create disposable projects, temporary sheets or scratch designs without checking the existing inventory first. The companion generate_unique_project_name and generate_unique_folder_name build unique file paths.
tools.usage:
from ansys.aedt.core.generic.general_methods import generate_unique_name, generate_unique_project_name, generate_unique_folder_name
name = generate_unique_name(root_name, suffix="", n=6)
path = generate_unique_project_name(root_name=None, folder_name=None, project_name=None, project_format="aedt")

parameters.name: root_name
parameters.description: Prefix of the generated name.

parameters.name: suffix
parameters.description: Optional string inserted between root and random part.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of random characters (default 6).

tools.example:
from ansys.aedt.core import Hfss
from ansys.aedt.core.generic.general_methods import generate_unique_name, generate_unique_project_name

proj = generate_unique_project_name(root_name="scan", folder_name="C:/work/tmp")
hfss = Hfss(project=proj, non_graphical=True)
sheet = hfss.modeler.create_rectangle("XY", [0, 0, 0], [1, 1], name=generate_unique_name("PortSheet"))
tools.notes: Random suffixes make names non-deterministic; for reproducible models pass explicit names and only use the generator for temporaries. Other helpers in the same module include open_file, read_json/read_toml (file_utils) and is_linux / is_windows flags.

tools.name: PyAEDT installation (pip install pyaedt, add_pyaedt_to_aedt)
tools.description: PyAEDT is installed as a normal Python package and does not ship with AEDT (except that recent releases bundle a copy in their CPython). The base package needs only a supported CPython; the [all] extra adds plotting (pyvista, matplotlib), pandas, scikit-rf for Touchstone processing and the PDF report generator; [dotnet] adds the pythonnet COM backend for old releases. add_pyaedt_to_aedt registers the PyAEDT panels in the AEDT ribbon so the same interpreter can be used from inside the desktop.
tools.usage:
pip install pyaedt
pip install pyaedt[all]
pip install pyaedt[dotnet]
conda install -c conda-forge pyaedt
python -c "from ansys.aedt.core.extensions.installer.pyaedt_installer import add_pyaedt_to_aedt; add_pyaedt_to_aedt('2025.1')"

parameters.name: Python versions
parameters.description: CPython 3.10 to 3.13 (check the release notes; AEDT's own CPython under <install>/commonfiles/CPython can be used on Windows and Linux).

parameters.name: AEDT versions
parameters.description: 2022 R1 and later, including the Student edition; gRPC needs 2022 R2+.

parameters.name: Offline install
parameters.description: pip install --no-index --find-links=<wheelhouse dir> pyaedt[all] using the wheelhouse archives published with each release.

parameters.name: PyAEDT Installer script
parameters.description: A .py file run through Tools > Run Script inside AEDT creates a virtual environment with AEDT's CPython and installs PyAEDT plus the ribbon panels.

tools.example:
# Windows PowerShell
py -3.11 -m venv C:\venv\pyaedt
C:\venv\pyaedt\Scripts\pip install pyaedt[all]
C:\venv\pyaedt\Scripts\python -c "import ansys.aedt.core as a; print(a.__version__)"

# Linux cluster login node, headless
python3 -m pip install --user pyaedt
export ANSYSEM_ROOT251=/opt/ansys_inc/v251/AnsysEM
python3 -c "from ansys.aedt.core import Hfss; h=Hfss(version='2025.1', non_graphical=True); print(h.aedt_version_id); h.release_desktop()"
tools.notes: The import path is ansys.aedt.core since v0.10; `import pyaedt` still works through a shim but is deprecated. On Linux set ANSYSEM_ROOT<ver> (or let PyAEDT detect the installation) and make sure the display-less session uses non_graphical=True. PyEDB (pip install pyedb) is a separate package that PyAEDT installs as a dependency.

tools.name: Automation tab: PyAEDT Console / Jupyter Notebook / Run PyAEDT Script
tools.description: Once PyAEDT is registered in AEDT (add_pyaedt_to_aedt or the installer script), the Automation ribbon tab and Tools > Toolkit > PersonalLib gain three buttons: Console opens an interactive CPython console already connected to the active project and design (with hfss/app objects predefined), Jupyter Notebook launches a notebook server bound to the session, and Run PyAEDT Script executes a chosen .py file against the open desktop. They are the interactive way to prototype PyAEDT code against a model that is being edited in the GUI.
tools.usage:
AEDT ribbon > Automation > Console | Jupyter Notebook | Run PyAEDT Script
Tools > Toolkit > PersonalLib > <same entries>

parameters.name: Console
parameters.description: Opens a terminal running the registered CPython with PyAEDT imported and an application object created for the active design (variable names such as hfss, m3d, cir depending on the design type).

parameters.name: Jupyter Notebook
parameters.description: Starts Jupyter in the browser with the same environment; the notebook connects with new_desktop=False.

parameters.name: Run PyAEDT Script
parameters.description: File browser to pick a script; it runs in the external CPython, not in AEDT's IronPython, so the full PyAEDT API and third-party packages are available.

tools.example:
# In the Automation > Console window (HFSS design active):
>>> hfss.design_name
'Patch'
>>> hfss.modeler.object_names
['Sub', 'Patch', 'Gnd', 'Region']
>>> hfss.post.create_report("dB(S(1,1))")

# A script launched with Run PyAEDT Script attaches like this:
from ansys.aedt.core import Hfss
hfss = Hfss(new_desktop=False)   # binds to the desktop that launched it
tools.notes: The buttons appear from AEDT 2023 R2 in the Automation tab; older releases show them only under Tools > Toolkit. Tools > Run Script (without 'PyAEDT') still runs IronPython/VBScript object-model scripts inside AEDT and cannot import ansys.aedt.core.

tools.name: Extension Manager (PyAEDT extensions)
tools.description: A panel in the Automation tab that installs and launches PyAEDT extensions: small GUI tools written on top of PyAEDT that run against the active design. They come in three flavours - pre-installed extensions, open-source PyAEDT toolkits from the ansys/pyaedt-toolkits repositories (for example the Antenna Toolkit and Magnet Segmentation), and custom extensions that point at a user's own Python script - and are pinned at project level (all applications) or at application level (HFSS, HFSS 3D Layout, Maxwell, Icepak, Circuit, Q3D, EMIT, Twin Builder).
tools.usage:
Automation > Extension Manager > choose Project or <Application> > install / launch
Standalone: python -m ansys.aedt.core.extensions.<app>.<extension_name>   (or the launch command shown in the docs)

parameters.name: Project-level extensions
parameters.description: Generate Report (PDF from the solved design), Result Calculator, Import Nastran, Advanced Fields Calculator, Point Cloud Generator.

parameters.name: HFSS extensions
parameters.description: Choke Designer, Push Excitation from File, Shielding Effectiveness, Move It (moving objects for Doppler), MCAD Assembly, Fresnel Coefficients.

parameters.name: HFSS 3D Layout extensions
parameters.description: Parametrize Layout, Configure Layout, Arbitrary Wave Port, Push Excitation from File, Via Design, Cutout, Export Layout, Export to 3D, Layout Design Toolkit.

parameters.name: Other applications
parameters.description: Maxwell: Fields Loss Distribution, Coil Design; Icepak: Create Power Map; Circuit: Schematic Import, Circuit Configuration; Q3D: Harmonic Loss Input; EMIT: Interference Classification, EMI Heat Map; Twin Builder: Convert to Circuit.

parameters.name: Custom extension
parameters.description: Any Python script; the manager creates the ribbon button and runs it with the registered interpreter.

tools.example:
# Steps
# 1. Automation > Extension Manager
# 2. Select 'HFSS' as destination, tick 'Shielding Effectiveness', Install
# 3. The button appears in the HFSS ribbon; click it with a design active
# 4. For a custom tool choose 'Custom', browse to C:/tools/my_sweep_gui.py, give it a name

# Running an extension standalone (no ribbon):
#   python -m ansys.aedt.core.extensions.hfss.shielding_effectiveness
tools.notes: Extensions need the PyAEDT panels installed first (add_pyaedt_to_aedt). The Antenna Toolkit (antenna synthesis wizard: patches, dipoles, horns, helices, Vivaldi, bowtie, etc., with parametrised 3D geometry) is installed as the 'ansys-aedt-toolkits-antenna' package and appears in the manager's toolkit list.
